subject: humanities
passage: Hand-knotted carpets from the Kashmir Valley are woven from a talim, a coded script that tells the weaver the color of every knot. Learning to read it is slow, and workshop owners often say that a weaver is not fully productive until several years into the trade. Textile scholar Nighat Mir, who timed weavers of different experience at a workshop near Srinagar, agrees that speed rises with experience, but she argues that most of the gain comes early: the largest jump, she contends, occurs within the first two years, after which weavers improve only gradually.

data.title: Weaving Speed by Experience at a Kashmiri Carpet Workshop

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mir's argument?

choices.A: Weavers with under 1 year of experience tied fewer than half as many knots per hour as those with more than 10 years.
choices.B: Knots per hour rose by roughly equal amounts from each experience group to the next.
choices.C: Knots per hour rose by 310 between the first year and the second, but by only 160 across all the more experienced groups combined.
choices.D: Weavers with more than 10 years of experience tied the most knots per hour, 880.

explanation.why: Mir does not dispute that experienced weavers are faster; her specific claim is about timing: the big jump comes in the first two years and later gains are gradual. To support it, compare the size of the increases between rows. From under 1 year to 1–2 years, speed rises 410 to 720 (310 knots); from 1–2 years to more than 10, it rises only 720 to 880 (160 knots).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (410 versus 880), but a comparison of the two extremes shows that speed rises with experience, not that most of the rise happens early.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The increases are 310, 70, 60, and 30 knots, which are far from equal.
explanation.C: Correct. A 310-knot jump in the first two years against a 160-knot rise over all the later years shows that most of the improvement comes early.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but the most experienced group being fastest is what the workshop owners also believe; it says nothing about when the gains occur.
